steps.body: You know the numeric version: 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4. Now let the base be a **variable**: x^(m/n) = ⁿ√(xᵐ). The denominator is the root, the numerator is the power — so x^(3/2) = √(x³), and ∛(x²) = x^(2/3). Two notations, one object.

options.label: x^(5/3)
options.feedback: Right — power 5 up top, root 3 underneath.

options.label: x^(3/5)
options.feedback: The fraction is power-over-root: the 5 (power) goes in the numerator.

options.label: x^(5·3)
options.feedback: Root and power don't multiply — they stack as a fraction: 5/3.

options.label: x^(5−3)
options.feedback: Nothing subtracts here — the root index becomes the DENOMINATOR: 5/3.

steps.body: Going the other way is just as mechanical: x^(4/5) = ⁵√(x⁴). And a unit fraction drops the power entirely: x^(1/2) = √x, x^(1/3) = ∛x. Exponent form is usually easier to **compute** with; radical form is easier to **read**.

explanationVariants: Numerator inside as the power, denominator outside as the root index.

commonBuilds.feedback: The DENOMINATOR 7 is the root index — the 2 is the power inside.
The 2 is an exponent on x, not a coefficient: x² under the seventh root.
Nothing adds the 2 and 7 — the form is (⁷√x)², power 2.

widget.missFeedback: The denominator of the exponent is the root index; the numerator is the power kept inside the radical.
widget.successFeedback: Right — seventh root of x squared.

commonErrors.feedback: 16 · 3/2 multiplies base by exponent — instead ROOT then POWER: (√16)³ = 4³ = 64.
That takes the FOURTH root (2³ = 8) — the denominator here is 2: (√16)³ = 4³ = 64.

explanationVariants: Read the invisible index: a bare √ is a 2nd root.

options.label: x^(5/2)
options.feedback: Right — the bare radical carries an invisible index 2.

options.label: x^(2/5)
options.feedback: Power-over-root: the 5 (power) is the numerator, the 2 (root) the denominator.

options.label: x^(5) − x^(2)
options.feedback: Roots never subtract exponents apart — they make one fraction: 5/2.

options.label: x^(10)
options.feedback: That multiplies 5 · 2 — the root DIVIDES the power: 5/2.

explanationVariants: x^(1/4) is the plain fourth root: ⁴√x.
Numerator 1 means no extra power — just the root.

commonBuilds.feedback: That's x^(4/2) = x² — the 4 here is the ROOT index, not a power.
An exponent of 1/4 takes a root — it never divides the base by 4.
That equals x itself — x^(1/4) has no power on the x inside.

widget.missFeedback: A 1/4 exponent is a pure root: index 4, with no power on the x inside.
widget.successFeedback: Right — a unit-fraction exponent is a bare root.

numericErrors.feedback: 12 is 3 · 4 — after the cube root gives 3, RAISE to the 4th: 81.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

hints: Denominator first: take the cube root of 27.

steps.body: x^(m/n) = ⁿ√(xᵐ): numerator powers, denominator roots.
takeaways: The root index becomes the exponent's denominator.
Unit fractions are bare roots: x^(1/n) = ⁿ√x.
Root first when evaluating — the numbers stay small.
steps.teaser: Next: the exponent rules you know — running on fractions.

concept.body: Read the fraction as instructions: in x^(m/n), the top m is the power, the bottom n is the root. For x^(3/4): power 3, root 4.

explanationVariants: ⁴√(x³) — fourth root of x cubed.
Numerator inside, denominator on the radical.

options.label: ⁴√(x³)
options.feedback: Right — power 3 under a fourth root.

options.label: ³√(x⁴)
options.feedback: The DENOMINATOR is the root: 4 goes on the radical, 3 inside as the power.

options.label: ⁴√(3x)
options.feedback: The 3 is a power on x (x³), not a multiplier.

options.label: √(x¾)
options.feedback: The whole fraction is the exponent — split it: root 4 outside, power 3 inside.
